claim: RecBCD is able to generate forces up to 25–40 pN without a significant effect on their velocity.
source: We show that RecBCD and its subunits are able to generate forces up to 25–40 pN without a significant effect on their velocity.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The isolated RecD translocates fast but is a weak helicase with limited processivity.
source: Moreover, the isolated RecD translocates fast but is a weak helicase with limited processivity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: RecD unwinds DNA as a Brownian ratchet, rectified by ATP binding.
source: Experiments at a broad range of [ATP] and forces suggest that RecD unwinds DNA as a Brownian ratchet, rectified by ATP binding, and that the presence of the other subunits shifts the ratchet equilibrium towards the post-translocation state.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by kinetic modeling and global fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of the other subunits shifts the ratchet equilibrium towards the post-translocation state.
source: Experiments at a broad range of [ATP] and forces suggest that RecD unwinds DNA as a Brownian ratchet, rectified by ATP binding, and that the presence of the other subunits shifts the ratchet equilibrium towards the post-translocation state.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by comparison of kinetic parameters between isolated RecD and RecD in complex, shown in Figure 5.

claim: RecBCD possesses a remarkable unwinding rate approaching ~ 1600 bp s−1.
source: Bulk and single molecule biochemical and biophysical studies of RecBCD revealed that it possesses a remarkable unwinding rate approaching ~ 1600 bp s−1 (Handa et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2013; Lucius et al., 2002; Roman and Kowalczykowski, 1989a; Xie et al., 2013), and real-time imaging of live E. coli cells has recently confirmed this result (Wiktor et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: RecBCD is able to evict or displace bound proteins or complexes, such as RNA polymerase, EcoRI, the lac repressor and even nucleosomes.
source: In these studies, it was shown that RecBCD is able to evict or displace bound proteins or complexes, such as RNA polymerase, EcoRI, the lac repressor and even nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Finkelstein et al., 2010.

claim: RecBCD did not pause during collisions with protein roadblocks and often pushed proteins thousands of base-pairs before evicting them from DNA.
source: RecBCD did not pause during these collisions and often pushed proteins thousands of base-pairs before evicting them from DNA.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies cited in the introduction.

claim: ~ 20–30 pN of force are required to evict RNA polymerase.
source: For example, single-molecule studies using DNA unzipping to probe DNA-bound proteins have shown that ~ 20–30 pN of force are required to evict RNA polymerase (Jin et al., 2010), nucleosomes (Hall et al., 2009; Rudnizky et al., 2016; ), and the Egr-1 transcription factor (Rudnizky et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jin et al., 2010.

claim: A previous single-molecule study reported that RecBCD is unable to translocate against forces higher than ~8 pN.
source: However, a previous single-molecule study reported that RecBCD is unable to translocate against forces higher than ~8 pN (Perkins et al., 2004), although these measurements were performed at very low ATP concentrations (<15 μM).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perkins et al., 2004.

claim: RecBCD binds the blunt end DNA resulting from the DSB and unwinds the DNA, primarily nicking the 3' tail.
source: First, RecBCD binds the blunt end DNA resulting from the DSB and unwinds the DNA, primarily nicking the 3' tail.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies cited in the introduction.

claim: The opposing translocation polarities of RecB and RecD allow them to simultaneously translocate on opposite strands of the DNA.
source: The opposing translocation polarities of RecB and RecD allow them to simultaneously translocate on opposite strands of the DNA (Dillingham et al., 2003; Taylor and Smith, 2003) but, since RecD is faster than RecB under physiological conditions (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008; Spies et al., 2007; Taylor and Smith, 2003), a single-stranded loop accumulates on the 3'-ended strand (Taylor and Smith, 2003; Wong et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: RecD is faster than RecB under physiological conditions.
source: The opposing translocation polarities of RecB and RecD allow them to simultaneously translocate on opposite strands of the DNA (Dillingham et al., 2003; Taylor and Smith, 2003) but, since RecD is faster than RecB under physiological conditions (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008; Spies et al., 2007; Taylor and Smith, 2003), a single-stranded loop accumulates on the 3'-ended strand (Taylor and Smith, 2003; Wong et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A single-stranded loop accumulates on the 3'-ended strand.
source: The opposing translocation polarities of RecB and RecD allow them to simultaneously translocate on opposite strands of the DNA (Dillingham et al., 2003; Taylor and Smith, 2003) but, since RecD is faster than RecB under physiological conditions (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008; Spies et al., 2007; Taylor and Smith, 2003), a single-stranded loop accumulates on the 3'-ended strand (Taylor and Smith, 2003; Wong et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RecBCD is able to generate a high force (43 ± 2 pN).
source: Hence, Figure 2a indicates that RecBCD is able to generate a high force (43 ± 2 pN; Fitted force for half-maximal velocity ± standard error).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: RecB is able to generate similar forces (40 ± 3 pN).
source: Interestingly, although RecB is able to generate similar forces (40 ± 3 pN; Figure 2c), the maximal forces generated by RecD are ~ 30% smaller (29 ± 3 pN; Figure 2b), suggesting that this subunit, by itself, is unable to generate the maximal forces observed for RecBCD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The maximal forces generated by RecD are ~ 30% smaller (29 ± 3 pN).
source: Interestingly, although RecB is able to generate similar forces (40 ± 3 pN; Figure 2c), the maximal forces generated by RecD are ~ 30% smaller (29 ± 3 pN; Figure 2b), suggesting that this subunit, by itself, is unable to generate the maximal forces observed for RecBCD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: RecD, by itself, is unable to generate the maximal forces observed for RecBCD.
source: Interestingly, although RecB is able to generate similar forces (40 ± 3 pN; Figure 2c), the maximal forces generated by RecD are ~ 30% smaller (29 ± 3 pN; Figure 2b), suggesting that this subunit, by itself, is unable to generate the maximal forces observed for RecBCD.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of force measurements for RecBCD and RecD.

claim: Both subunits unwind DNA at ~400 bp/s at low forces.
source: At low forces, experiments with the asymmetric constructs reveal that both subunits unwind DNA at ~400 bp/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from asymmetric constructs.

claim: Experiments probing the whole complex show an unwinding rate of ~1100 bp/s.
source: Experiments probing the whole complex, where each subunit unwinds a different track, show an unwinding rate of ~1100 bp/s, significantly higher than the sum of the rates measured for the individual subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the symmetric construct.

claim: The unwinding rate of the whole complex is significantly higher than the sum of the rates measured for the individual subunits.
source: Experiments probing the whole complex, where each subunit unwinds a different track, show an unwinding rate of ~1100 bp/s, significantly higher than the sum of the rates measured for the individual subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data.

claim: RecD showed poor processivity (~ 50 bps).
source: RecD showed poor processivity (~ 50 bps), in accordance with previous measurements (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: RecBCD has a processivity of ~ 30,000 bp.
source: When compared with the reported ~ 30,000 bp processivity of RecBCD (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008), this indicates that the presence of RecC and/or RecB, perhaps acting as a 'toehold' as previously proposed (Carter et al., 2016), is required to fully achieve RecBCD's processivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008.

claim: The presence of RecC and/or RecB is required to fully achieve RecBCD's processivity.
source: When compared with the reported ~ 30,000 bp processivity of RecBCD (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008), this indicates that the presence of RecC and/or RecB, perhaps acting as a 'toehold' as previously proposed (Carter et al., 2016), is required to fully achieve RecBCD's processivity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of processivity measurements.

claim: While RecD in complex can unwind and translocate at very fast rates (~430 bp/s), the isolated subunit is practically unable to unwind the fork.
source: However, comparing RecD's activity in both configurations, extrapolated to zero force, reveals a significant difference (Figure 3d): while RecD in complex can unwind and translocate at very fast rates (~430 bp/s), the isolated subunit is practically unable to unwind the fork.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The presence of the RecC and/or RecB subunits is necessary for the RecD subunit to efficiently and processively unwind DNA.
source: Thus, we conclude that the presence of the RecC and/or RecB subunits is necessary for the RecD subunit to efficiently and processively unwind DNA.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing isolated RecD to RecD in complex.

claim: RecD's step size is ~3 bps.
source: First, they reveal that RecD's step size is ~3 bps, which is in accordance with previously reported step sizes characterized by RecBCD when RecD is the leading subunit (before the Chi sequence) (Lucius et al., 2002) but, surprisingly, not with the 1 bp step size reported for the related SF1 helicase UvrD (Lee and Yang, 2006).
evidence: This claim is derived from global fitting of kinetic models to experimental data.

claim: The only profound effect of being in complex is reflected in shifting the equilibrium of the ratchet towards the post translocation state, by approximately 200-fold.
source: Remarkably, comparing the rate constants resulting from the global fitting, for RecD in complex and when isolated, revealed that most microscopic rates are not greatly affected, and that the only profound effect of being in complex is reflected in shifting the equilibrium of the ratchet towards the post translocation state, by approximately 200-fold (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of kinetic parameters shown in Figure 5.

claim: RecB is a 134 kDa, 3'−5' helicase.
source: RecBCD possesses three subunits, two of which are super-family one helicases: RecB, a 134 kDa, 3'−5' helicase and RecD, a 67 kDa helicase with 5'−3' polarity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RecB structure and function.

claim: RecD is a 67 kDa helicase with 5'−3' polarity.
source: RecBCD possesses three subunits, two of which are super-family one helicases: RecB, a 134 kDa, 3'−5' helicase and RecD, a 67 kDa helicase with 5'−3' polarity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RecD structure and function.

claim: The RecC subunit is a 128 kDa, catalytically dead helicase-nuclease sharing a similar structure to RecB.
source: The RecC subunit is a 128 kDa, catalytically dead helicase-nuclease sharing a similar structure to RecB, which acts as a scaffold protein stapling RecB and RecD (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008), and is responsible for recognition of the regulatory Chi sequence (Handa et al., 2012; Singleton et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RecC structure and function, supported by citations.

claim: RecC acts as a scaffold protein stapling RecB and RecD.
source: The RecC subunit is a 128 kDa, catalytically dead helicase-nuclease sharing a similar structure to RecB, which acts as a scaffold protein stapling RecB and RecD (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008), and is responsible for recognition of the regulatory Chi sequence (Handa et al., 2012; Singleton et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008.

claim: RecC is responsible for recognition of the regulatory Chi sequence.
source: The RecC subunit is a 128 kDa, catalytically dead helicase-nuclease sharing a similar structure to RecB, which acts as a scaffold protein stapling RecB and RecD (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008), and is responsible for recognition of the regulatory Chi sequence (Handa et al., 2012; Singleton et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Handa et al., 2012 and Singleton et al., 2004.

claim: The crystal structure of RecBCD's initiation complex shows that 4–6 bps of DNA are unwound at the 'pin' domain of RecC.
source: The crystal structure of RecBCD's initiation complex shows that 4–6 bps of DNA are unwound at the 'pin' domain of RecC after which the split strands are directed towards the helicase subunits, RecB and RecD (Singleton et al., 2004; Wilkinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: An 'arm' domain of RecB interacts with the DNA 12 bps ahead.
source: In addition, an 'arm' domain of RecB interacts with the DNA 12 bps ahead (Saikrishnan et al., 2008; Singleton et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: RecBCD's affinity towards DNA lacking a double stranded end is 10^6-fold weaker than that for blunt ends or short overhangs.
source: Unfortunately, this assay is not appropriate for the study of RecBCD since, in line with its biological function that requires binding to DSB sites, RecBCD's affinity towards DNA lacking a double stranded end is 106-fold weaker than that for blunt ends or short overhangs (Bianco et al., 2001; Roman and Kowalczykowski, 1989a; Taylor and Smith, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RecB possesses a 'secondary' translocase activity which translocates on DNA in the 5'→3' direction.
source: Recent studies have shown that RecB possesses a 'secondary' translocase activity (Wu et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2013), which translocates on DNA in the 5'→3' direction, that is with an opposite polarity with respect to its 'primary' translocase.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RecBK29QCD is deficient in RecB's ATPase activity and was shown to be inactive for both translocases (primary and secondary) of RecB.
source: To test whether the secondary translocase contributes to the activity observed in our measurements, we expressed and purified the mutant RecBK29QCD, which is deficient in RecB's ATPase activity and was shown to be inactive for both translocases (primary and secondary) of RecB (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2013.

claim: The measured force-velocity curves for RecBCD and RecBK29QCD on the asymmetric construct designed to probe RecD are indistinguishable.
source: However, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a shows that the measured force-velocity curves are indistinguishable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: RecBC can sustain maximal forces of only ~9 pN's.
source: In addition, we measured the activity of the RecBC complex, lacking the RecD subunit. Although we were able to follow its activity in our assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), our measurements show that it can sustain maximal forces of only ~9 pN's, suggesting that the secondary translocase is not able to maintain its grip of the DNA, and therefore not active, at higher forces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The secondary translocase is not able to maintain its grip of the DNA, and therefore not active, at higher forces.
source: In addition, we measured the activity of the RecBC complex, lacking the RecD subunit. Although we were able to follow its activity in our assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), our measurements show that it can sustain maximal forces of only ~9 pN's, suggesting that the secondary translocase is not able to maintain its grip of the DNA, and therefore not active, at higher forces.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the low force measurements for RecBC.

claim: The measurements are able to probe separately the activities of RecB and RecD as they are part of a full complex.
source: Taken together, this indicates that our measurements are indeed able to probe separately the activities of RecB and RecD as they are part of a full complex.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental validation with mutants.

claim: The 2–3 fold higher velocity previously measured for RecBCD relative to its subunits indicates some degree of synergy between them.
source: This is in line with previous experiments showing that, while each of the subunits (RecB, RecD) is capable of independently catalyzing unwinding, neither of the subunits alone can reach the unwinding rates of RecBCD (Dillingham et al., 2005; Pavankumar et al., 2010; Taylor and Smith, 2003; Xie et al., 2013). The 2–3 fold higher velocity previously measured for RecBCD relative to its subunits indicates some degree of synergy between them.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies and comparison of velocities.

claim: At least part of the synergy effect results from direct allosteric interactions between the subunits.
source: Our results, which show a 1.4-fold faster activity when both subunits are present but unwinding different substrates, suggest that at least part of this effect results from direct allosteric interactions between the subunits.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observation of increased velocity when both subunits are active.

claim: The observed lengths of the unwinding traces (490 ± 13 bp, 116 ± 16 bp and 380 ± 43 bp, mean ± s.e.m, for RecBCD, RecD and RecB, respectively) do not represent the processivity of the enzyme or its subunits.
source: Finally, since the traces in our experiments are terminated by the force-induced dissociation of the complex from DNA, the observed lengths of the unwinding traces (490 ± 13 bp, 116 ± 16 bp and 380 ± 43 bp, mean ± s.e.m, for RecBCD, RecD and RecB, respectively) do not represent the processivity of the enzyme or its subunits.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated as a caveat about the interpretation of the data.

claim: A previous single-molecule study reported on extensive conformational dynamics of the RecBCD-DNA complex, arising from back-and-forth motion of the enzyme relative dsDNA.
source: Interestingly, a previous single-molecule study reported on extensive conformational dynamics of the RecBCD-DNA complex, arising from back-and-forth motion of the enzyme relative dsDNA (Carter et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carter et al., 2016.

claim: The conformational dynamics were observed in the absence of ATP and depend on the GC content of the DNA, but are suppressed by a non-hydrolyzable ATP analog.
source: These dynamics were observed in the absence of ATP and depend on the GC content of the DNA, but are suppressed by a non-hydrolyzable ATP analog.
evidence: This claim is based on previous work by Carter et al., 2016.

claim: RecD is the leading helicase before the Chi sequence.
source: Given that RecD is the leading helicase before the Chi sequence (Liu et al., 2013; Spies et al., 2007) and in view of our results, it is possible that the previously observed dynamics represent the fluctuations of RecD between its pre- and post-translocation states.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The previously observed dynamics may represent the fluctuations of RecD between its pre- and post-translocation states.
source: Given that RecD is the leading helicase before the Chi sequence (Liu et al., 2013; Spies et al., 2007) and in view of our results, it is possible that the previously observed dynamics represent the fluctuations of RecD between its pre- and post-translocation states.
evidence: This claim is speculative, connecting previous observations with the current findings.

claim: The forces measured here provide a mechanical basis for RecBCD's ability to overcome DNA-bound proteins.
source: Considering the typical forces required to displace DNA-bound proteins, as measured by unzipping the DNA (Jiang et al., 2005; Koch and Wang, 2003; Koch et al., 2002; Meng et al., 2017; Rudnizky et al., 2018) or by using a second DNA molecule as a probe (Noom et al., 2007), our measurements provide a mechanical basis for the ability of RecBCD to overcome protein 'roadblocks' (Finkelstein et al., 2010; Gorman and Greene, 2008; Terakawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of measured forces with known forces required to displace proteins.

claim: The differences in force measurements may be related to the different chemical conditions at which the experiments were performed.
source: These differences may be related to the different chemical conditions at which the experiments were performed.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for differences with previous studies.

claim: At very low ATP concentrations, the enzyme spends most of the time fluctuating between the pre- and post-translocation states.
source: Under these conditions, the enzyme spends most of the time fluctuating between the pre- and post-translocation states, waiting for an ATP molecule that can 'lock' it in the post-translocation state and allow it to continue the catalytic cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic model and the effect of low ATP.

claim: The dynamic states (pre-translocation and post-translocation with no ATP bound) are likely characterized by weaker protein-DNA interactions.
source: These dynamic states (pre-translocation and post-translocation with no ATP bound) are likely characterized by weaker protein-DNA interactions and thus particularly sensitive to an applied force.
evidence: This is speculation about the nature of the dynamic states.

claim: Higher [ATP] allows the enzyme to minimize the time it spends in the force-sensitive states, thus reaching much higher forces.
source: Higher [ATP] allows the enzyme to minimize the time it spends in the force-sensitive states, thus reaching much higher forces.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic model and experimental observations.

claim: The formation of the loop may have a significant effect in the biotinylated RecBCD setup previously reported.
source: The formation of the loop may have a significant effect in the biotinylated RecBCD setup previously reported, and might be the reason for RecBCD's slippage against forces larger than ~8 pN (Perkins et al., 2004).
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for differences with previous studies.

claim: In the current setup, where each subunit unwinds a different dsDNA segment, no loop formation takes place.
source: In our setup, where each subunit unwinds a different dsDNA segment, no loop formation takes place.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The loop formation may have a potential regulatory role.
source: Interestingly, if this is the reason for the differences observed, it may stress the potential regulatory role of the loop.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological significance of loop formation.

claim: The helicase subunits function by a division of labor throughout the unwinding reaction.
source: This supports a model in which the helicase subunits function by a division of labor throughout the unwinding reaction.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: While the helicase subunits pull the DNA, they seem to play a very minor role in destabilizing the fork.
source: While the helicase subunits pull the DNA, they seem to play a very minor role in destabilizing the fork.
evidence: This is inferred from the low destabilization energy measured for RecD.

claim: The effect of the additional units on RecD may be mediated by two structural motifs in the RecBCD complex.
source: We speculate that this effect may be mediated by two structural motifs in the RecBCD complex.
evidence: This is speculation about the structural basis for the observed effects.

claim: RecC has a pin that separates the complex, sending each strand into the RecB and RecD subunits.
source: First, it has been shown that RecC has a pin that separates the complex, sending each strand into the RecB and RecD subunits (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008; Singleton et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: RecBCD can unwind duplex DNA processively in the absence of ssDNA translocation by the canonical motors.
source: Second, a recent work suggested that RecBCD can unwind duplex DNA processively in the absence of ssDNA translocation by the canonical motors (Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Simon et al., 2016.

claim: The arm protrusion in RecB may play a role in destabilizing the fork.
source: This was related to the arm protrusion in RecB that interacts with the double-stranded DNA ahead, which may also play a role in destabilizing the fork.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural features and previous work.

claim: A common feature of structural models for DNA unwinding by helicases is that melting occurs as the ssDNA translocase pulls the duplex DNA against a protein wedge or pin at the ss/dsDNA junction.
source: In fact, a common feature of structural models for DNA unwinding by helicases is that melting occurs as the ssDNA translocase pulls the duplex DNA against a protein wedge or pin at the ss/dsDNA junction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about helicase mechanisms.

claim: For RecBCD, the structure of the full complex suggests that the pin is in RecC.
source: For RecBCD, the structure of the full complex suggests that the pin is in RecC (Singleton et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: The assays allow us to experimentally demonstrate a functional role for the presence of the other subunits.
source: By comparing the activity of the RecD subunit, when it is part of a wild-type, complete RecBCD complex to its activity in isolation, our assays allow us to experimentally demonstrate a functional role for the presence of the other subunits.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the work.

claim: In the normal operation of RecBCD, two complementary strands are translocated by the two subunits, RecB and RecD.
source: Normally, as a DNA molecule is unwound by RecBCD, two complementary strands are translocated by the two subunits, RecB and RecD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RecBCD function.

claim: In the current assay, each of the helicase subunits (RecB and RecD) unwinds a separate dsDNA segment.
source: In our assay, each of the helicase subunits (RecB and RecD) unwinds a separate dsDNA segment and therefore a structural element normally destabilizing the fork cannot be simultaneously destabilizing the two DNA segments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A structural element normally destabilizing the fork cannot be simultaneously destabilizing the two DNA segments in the current assay.
source: In our assay, each of the helicase subunits (RecB and RecD) unwinds a separate dsDNA segment and therefore a structural element normally destabilizing the fork cannot be simultaneously destabilizing the two DNA segments.
evidence: This is a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: The experiments clearly demonstrate that RecBCD unwinds the DNA.
source: On the other hand, our experiments clearly demonstrate that RecBCD unwinds the DNA (Figure 2a), and that it does so by exploiting the unwinding activity of both helicases, RecB and RecD (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: RecBCD unwinds DNA by exploiting the unwinding activity of both helicases, RecB and RecD.
source: On the other hand, our experiments clearly demonstrate that RecBCD unwinds the DNA (Figure 2a), and that it does so by exploiting the unwinding activity of both helicases, RecB and RecD (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b,c.

claim: There may be more than one structural element catalyzing unwinding in RecBCD.
source: One possible way to reconcile these observations is that there is more than one structural element catalyzing unwinding, and that in our assay at least one of them assists the unwinding by RecB, while at least another one assist RecD.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism to reconcile observations.

claim: RecBCD can fluctuate between two different conformations: one in which structural elements assist unwinding of the dsDNA in RecB, and a conformation that allows unwinding of the DNA in RecD.
source: A different explanation, which we favor, is that RecBCD can fluctuate between two different conformations: one in which the pin, or other structural elements, are positioned to assist unwinding of the dsDNA in RecB, and therefore no unwinding takes place by RecD, and a conformation that allows unwinding of the DNA in RecD, but not the one in RecB.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the observations.

claim: The subunits alternate between active and inactive states, thus their average velocity is slower than the velocity under normal operation.
source: As a result, since the subunits alternate between active and inactive states, their average velocity is slower than the velocity under normal operation, thus meaning that our assay underestimates the unwinding velocities.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequence of the proposed conformational fluctuations.

claim: The assay may underestimate the unwinding velocities.
source: As a result, since the subunits alternate between active and inactive states, their average velocity is slower than the velocity under normal operation, thus meaning that our assay underestimates the unwinding velocities.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the measurements.

claim: The possible underestimation does not affect the conclusions about force response.
source: However, this possible underestimation does not affect our conclusions.
evidence: This is an argument about the validity of the conclusions despite the limitation.

claim: The velocities measured are just multiplied by a constant factor due to the assay design.
source: First, the velocities measured are just multiplied by a constant factor: In the first possible scenario, this is the partial degree of destabilization offered by having only a subset of the destabilizing elements for each subunit. In the second scenario, this is the fraction of the time RecBCD spends in each of the conformations.
evidence: This is an argument about how the assay limitation affects the measurements.

claim: The functional dependence of the velocity on the force as measured truly represents the force response of the whole enzyme and its subunits.
source: Up to this numerical constant, the functional dependence of the velocity on the force as we measure truly represents the force response of the whole enzyme and its subunits.
evidence: This is an argument about the validity of the force-velocity relationships measured.

claim: The underestimation of RecD velocity in the in-complex assay only strengthens the fact that the zero-force extrapolations are in disagreement.
source: Specifically, for RecD, the underestimation of its velocity in the in-complex assay only strengthens the fact that at the zero-force extrapolation of Figure 2b (>400 bp/s) and Figure 3c (~0 bp/s) are in disagreement, and suggest the existence of a destabilizing element in the complex.
evidence: This is an argument about how the limitation affects the interpretation of the data.

claim: Additional, weak ATP-binding sites beyond the catalytic ones in RecB and RecD serve as auxiliary sites from which ATP is transferred to the catalytic sites.
source: In a recent work, we showed that this fast rate is supported by additional, weak ATP-binding sites, beyond the catalytic ones in RecB and RecD, that serve as auxiliary sites from which ATP is transferred to the catalytic sites.
evidence: This claim is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: The auxiliary ATP-binding sites result in a significant increase in RecBCD's unwinding velocity at intermediate ATP concentrations.
source: This mechanism was shown to result in a significant increase in RecBCD's unwinding velocity at intermediate ATP concentrations (Zananiri et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: It is possible that the existence of the auxiliary sites and the results presented here are related.
source: It is possible that the existence of the auxiliary sites and the results presented here are related: In the case of a BR coupled to ATP binding, an opposing force such as an externally applied force or a DNA-binding protein presenting a roadblock for translocation, decreases the rate of reaching the post-translocation state, and therefore the rate of ATP binding.
evidence: This is speculation about the connection between auxiliary sites and force response.

claim: The ATP auxiliary sites may play a role in overcoming the effect of the force, by allowing binding via a parallel pathway.
source: Hence, it is possible that the ATP auxiliary sites play a role in overcoming the effect of the force, by allowing binding via a parallel pathway.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of auxiliary sites.
